scenario: AITA for wanting my girlfriend to be less braggy about her work perks? She seems to forget that the way she lives isn't how most people live... | My girlfriend has a pretty sweet job. She doesn't have set hours; she just has to work 35 hours a week whenever is convenient for her and make it to her few meetings. She can work from the office or from home sometimes. She has a full benefits package despite being under what most people consider full time. A really nice retirement package too. And the company will pay everything for continued education. She does work she finds interesting (cutting edge robotics) and gets along well with her coworkers. She has a lot of PTO per year and her boss even lets the employees "earn up" more; if they work extra hours one week they can ask for the equivalent in PTO for later. Her team's managers buy them whatever they want for the office; they want a 500 dollar expresso maker, they get it. They want a type of fancy coffee, they get it. Nice furniture, done... They get paid well too; pretty middle of the road salary for robotics but she says the work life balance more than makes up for it. She'd rather have more time than be a top earner. And honestly a midrange robotics salary is still damn good. And anyway, For a while I thought "good for her" for having found something that she is happy with. But recently it's gotten frustrating because I think she forgets that this isn't how everyone lives. Like when we're out with my friends or just hanging out she'll talk about the nice stuff her managers bought for the office, about all the vacations she takes, about how she and her coworkers left the office in the middle of the day to see a movie then came back and just worked a little later. And yeah, it seems like she forgets that is no way a normal job. So last night we were at a party and she mentioned how she was going to tour a few new apartments Monday morning and afternoon, and one of the people at the party was like "don't you have work" and she said "yeah but I can set my own hours" And that just rubbed me the wrong way and I said that she needed to stop going on and on about her work perks, it was obnoxious and came off braggy. She was like "I was just explaining something" and I said it wasn't just this, it was everything. Most people don't live the life she lives." She said that I was coming off jealous and that it was a bad look. That she was where she was because she didn't settle for less; she studied and worked her ass off, and didn't let herself get too settled anywhere she was unfulfilled. And that instead of complaining, maybe I should ask myself what I'm feeling jealous of and what I need to do to get it. I told her she was missing the point; she'll always be around people who don't have what she does, and she could be a little more modest about it. She said I was the only one who seemed to have a problem with it, and stormed off... AITA for what I said?

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. The user wants me to evaluate whether the person's action is morally acceptable, and if so, answer 1, otherwise 0. The scenario is about someone who is frustrated with their girlfriend talking about her work perks, which they feel is braggy and forgets that not everyone has such a lifestyle.

First, I need to understand the situation. The girlfriend has a great job with flexible hours, good benefits, nice office perks, and a good salary. She's happy with her job and shares these details with friends. The person feels that she's bragging and forgets that not everyone has such a job. They confronted her about it, saying she should be more modest. She responded by saying they're jealous and should work on themselves instead of complaining.

Now, I need to determine if the person's action of telling her to stop talking about her work perks is morally acceptable. To do this, I should consider the moral principles involved. The main issue here is about modesty, bragging, and how one's behavior affects others.

On one hand, the person feels that their girlfriend is being obnoxious by constantly talking about her job perks. They argue that she should be more aware of others' situations and not flaunt her privileges. This could be seen as a desire for her to be more considerate and empathetic towards others who might not have such opportunities.

On the other hand, the girlfriend feels that she's just sharing her experiences and that she earned her job through hard work. She's proud of her achievements and doesn't see anything wrong with talking about them. She also accuses the person of being jealous and suggests they should focus on their own goals instead of being critical.

So, is it morally acceptable for the person to ask their girlfriend to be less braggy? I think it depends on how the request was made and the context in which it was delivered. If the person expressed their feelings respectfully and explained why they felt that way, it could be seen as a constructive criticism aimed at improving the relationship and mutual understanding.

However, if the person came across as accusatory or made the girlfriend feel defensive, it might not be the best approach. It's important to communicate feelings in a way that fosters understanding rather than defensiveness.

In this case, the person did express their frustration, but the girlfriend felt attacked and accused of being jealous. This suggests that the way the person communicated their feelings might have been harsh or insensitive. While the intention was to address a behavior that was bothering them, the method could be seen as lacking empathy.

Therefore, while the underlying concern about modesty and consideration is valid, the way the person addressed it might not have been the most morally acceptable approach. It's important to communicate such feelings in a way that is respectful and understanding, rather than accusatory.

So, considering all this, I would lean towards the action being morally unacceptable because the way it was communicated could be seen as insensitive and not constructive. It's better to approach such conversations with empathy and a focus on mutual understanding rather than making the other person feel defensive.
